title: Primary & secondary survey — unconscious RTA patient (ATLS)
scenario: A 25-year-old man had a car accident and was brought to the ER unconscious. Vitals: low BP, rapid respiratory rate. A trauma manikin is in the room. 430A
A trauma patient in the ER. 439F

qs.q: How will you manage him? (Primary survey — ABCDE in detail)
a: A — Airway with C-spine protection: talk to the patient ("What's your name?" — answering = patent airway + brain perfusion). If not: jaw thrust (no head tilt), suction. Unconscious (GCS ≤ 8) → definitive airway (intubation) with in-line C-spine immobilisation.

B — Breathing: expose the chest; RR, SpO₂, chest expansion, trachea, percussion, auscultation. Treat life-threats now: tension pneumothorax, open pneumothorax, massive haemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade.

C — Circulation: stop external bleeding; skin colour, temperature, capillary refill, pulse, BP, level of consciousness. 2 large-bore IV lines (14–16 G) and draw blood at the same time (cross- match, ABG — lactate & base deficit, CBC, U&E, coagulation, toxicology). 1 L warm crystalloid, then blood early if still unstable.
Hypotensive + tachycardic → start blood transfusion and look for the source: chest (CXR), abdomen (FAST), pelvis (X-ray), long bones, "the street" (external).
D — Disability: GCS, pupils (size/reactivity), lateralising signs.
E — Exposure: fully undress, log-roll, prevent hypothermia.
qs.why: ATLS treats what kills first: an obstructed airway kills in minutes, then breathing, then bleeding. So you go strictly A → B → C → D → E, treating each problem as you find it before moving on, and protect the C-spine throughout because an unconscious trauma patient has a spinal injury until proven otherwise.

qs.q: The examiner gives you the patient's responses — calculate the GCS.
a: Eyes 4 · Verbal 5 · Motor 6 (see table). Minor 13–15, moderate 9–12, severe ≤ 8 (→ intubate).
qs.why: GCS is the standard, reproducible measure of consciousness; the total (3–15) grades the head injury and decides the airway — GCS ≤ 8 means he can't protect his airway, so he needs intubation.

qs.q: The patient now has a unilateral fixed, dilated pupil — what will you do?
a: Urgent non-contrast CT head (→ see "Extradural haematoma" in Neurosurgery).
qs.why: A unilateral fixed dilated pupil means the third nerve is compressed by an expanding haematoma (uncal herniation). A non-contrast CT head is the fastest way to find the bleed so neurosurgery can evacuate it.

qs.q: What are the adjuncts to the primary survey?
a: Monitoring (ECG, SpO₂, BP), ABG.
Urinary catheter (if no urethral injury) and gastric tube (orogastric if head/facial injury).
Imaging: CXR, pelvic X-ray, eFAST.
qs.why: Adjuncts give objective information during the primary survey without moving the patient: monitors and ABG show perfusion, catheter output tracks resuscitation, and CXR, pelvic X-ray and eFAST find the hidden sources of bleeding.

qs.q: The patient is stable after the primary survey — what next?
a: Secondary survey: AMPLE history + full head-to-toe examination (log-roll, back, perineum), tetanus prophylaxis, identify all injuries.
qs.why: The secondary survey is only started once life-threats are controlled; the AMPLE history and head-to-toe exam (including the back by log-roll) pick up injuries missed in the rush of the primary survey.

qs.q: If you need imaging, what will you order?
a: Whole-body (pan-)CT once haemodynamically stable.
qs.why: A pan-CT is quick and comprehensive, but the scanner is no place for an unstable patient — so imaging comes only after he is haemodynamically stable.

qs.q: What can prolonged bleeding cause?
a: Lethal triad: hypothermia, coagulopathy, metabolic acidosis.
qs.why: Ongoing bleeding with cold fluids leads to hypothermia, dilution and consumption of clotting factors, and lactic acidosis — each worsens the others (the lethal triad), which is why we warm fluids and transfuse early.

qs.q: How do you know you gave enough fluid?
a: Urine output (adult ≥ 0.5 mL/kg/h), capillary refill time (+ HR, BP, mental status, lactate).
qs.why: Urine output reflects kidney perfusion, the best bedside sign that the circulation is adequately restored; capillary refill, falling heart rate, mental status and clearing lactate confirm it.

tips.t: Don't forget to say you will call the neurosurgeon / trauma team.

notes.t: The primary survey was also the first question in the 441F pelvic-fracture and 442A seat-belt stations (cases below).

title: Cervical spine injury — C5–C6 dislocation
scenario: Trauma patient with paraplegia and upper-limb weakness; lateral cervical X-ray shows dislocation at C5– C6. 436F
The unconscious RTA patient (above) turns out to have quadriplegia. Archive

imgs.cap: Lateral cervical spine X-ray — dislocation at C5–C6

qs.q: The patient has quadriplegia — where do you suspect the injury?
a: Cervical spinal cord.
qs.why: Paralysis of all four limbs means the lesion is above the arm segments (C5–T1), i.e. in the cervical cord.

qs.q: What is your next step in management?
a: Airway + C-spine immobilisation (collar/blocks), jaw thrust, intubation if needed.
Breathing: chest exam, RR, pulse oximetry.
Circulation: BP, HR, capillary refill, colour, temperature, stop any bleeding.
Disability: GCS and pupils.
Call / consult neurosurgery.
qs.why: Even with an obvious spinal injury, ATLS priorities don't change — high cervical injuries threaten breathing (phrenic nerve C3–5) and cause neurogenic shock, so ABCDE with spinal immobilisation comes first, then neurosurgery.

qs.q: What is the first investigation?
a: Lateral cervical spine X-ray (CT C-spine if available).
qs.why: A lateral C-spine film is quick and shows alignment; CT is more sensitive and is used when available.

qs.q: Read the X-ray.
a: Lateral view of the cervical spine showing dislocation of C5 on C6.
qs.why: Always name the view and level: the lateral film shows the anterior displacement of C5 over C6 — a dislocation.

qs.q: What other investigations would you order? (mention 2)
a: CT angiography (make sure the vessels are intact) and MRI spine (if stable); call the neurosurgeon.
qs.why: Cervical dislocations can injure the vertebral arteries (CT angiography), and MRI shows the cord and ligaments that X-ray and CT miss.

qs.q: How would you manage this patient? (mention 3)
a: Immobilise the spine (collar, brace).
Consult neurosurgery.
Definitive: surgical realignment, fixation and stabilisation.
qs.why: An unstable dislocation must be immobilised to prevent further cord damage, and definitively reduced and fixed by neurosurgery/spine surgery.

qs.q: What complications can cause death?
a: Pneumonia, respiratory distress/failure, sepsis, UTI.
qs.why: Late deaths after cord injury come from respiratory failure and pneumonia (weak respiratory muscles), sepsis and urinary infection (catheters, retention).

title: Rest station — bonus MCQs
scenario: The 442A/442B rest station had a bonus quiz of 4 easy MCQs.

qs.q: Stabbed in the chest, alert but short of breath, with a sucking wound — immediate management?
a: Cover the wound with a dressing taped on three sides (flutter valve); then a chest tube away from the wound.
qs.why: A three-sided dressing lets air out on expiration but not in on inspiration; taping all four sides can convert it into a tension pneumothorax.

qs.q: After an MVA: BP 80/50, tachycardic, FAST positive — next step?
a: Immediate exploratory laparotomy.
qs.why: An unstable patient with intra-abdominal blood is bleeding into the abdomen — CT is only for stable patients.

qs.q: Fever, RLQ pain and a tender mass; CT: 6 cm appendiceal abscess — management?
a: IV antibiotics + image-guided percutaneous drainage (± interval appendectomy).
qs.why: Operating on an inflamed mass is hazardous; draining the abscess and treating the infection settles it.

qs.q: Underweight young woman with vomiting and early satiety; CT: 3rd part of duodenum compressed between aorta and SMA — diagnosis?
a: Superior mesenteric artery syndrome (Wilkie's syndrome).
qs.why: Weight loss shrinks the fat pad between the aorta and SMA, narrowing the angle so the duodenum is compressed.

title: Blunt abdominal trauma — seat-belt sign & splenic injury
scenario: A 30-year-old restrained (seat-belted) driver after an MVA with severe abdominal and back pain; ecchymosis across the abdomen. (new case) 442A

qs.q: How would you manage this patient?
a: Primary survey in detail (ABCDE) + adjuncts: CXR, pelvic X-ray, labs, eFAST.
qs.why: Seat-belt sign means high-energy deceleration injury to the viscera — so start with ABCDE and use the adjuncts (eFAST, CXR, pelvic film) to find bleeding.

qs.q: Mention five areas of the eFAST.
a: Pericardial (subxiphoid), RUQ (hepatorenal), LUQ (splenorenal), suprapubic (pelvis), right and left anterior chest (pneumothorax).
qs.why: eFAST looks at the dependent spaces where blood collects (Morison's pouch, splenorenal, pelvis), the pericardium (tamponade), and both anterior chests (pneumothorax).

qs.q: Vitally stable, eFAST shows no haemoperitoneum, but severe LUQ pain with a seat-belt sign — what next?
a: CT abdomen (with IV contrast).
qs.why: In a stable patient a negative FAST doesn't exclude solid-organ injury; CT with IV contrast shows the injury and its grade, which decides management.

qs.q: CT shows a grade 3 splenic laceration with no contrast extravasation — management?
a: Conservative (non-operative) management: admit, monitor, serial examination and Hb.
qs.why: Stable patients with low/moderate-grade splenic injuries and no active bleeding do well without surgery — non-operative management preserves the spleen and its immune function.

qs.q: CT shows contrast extravasation and a grade 5 splenic laceration — what will you do?
a: Splenectomy.
qs.why: A shattered spleen (grade 5) or active contrast extravasation means ongoing haemorrhage — splenectomy (or embolisation in selected stable cases) stops it.

bonus.stem: A 40-year-old man after an MVA has BP 80/50 mmHg and tachycardia. FAST shows free fluid in the peritoneal cavity. What is the next best step?
opts: A. CT scan of the abdomen
D. Insert a central line and repeat FAST
bonus.ans: Answer: C — unstable + positive FAST = laparotomy (never send an unstable patient to CT).

title: Pelvic fracture — "open-book"
scenario: RTA patient with an open-book pelvic fracture. 441F

qs.q: Do the primary and secondary survey and manage the patient.
a: ABCDE with haemorrhage control: pelvic binder centred over the greater trochanters, 2 large- bore IV lines, massive-transfusion protocol (1:1:1); avoid repeated "springing" of the pelvis. Suspect urethral injury (blood at the meatus, high-riding prostate) → do not insert a Foley blindly; retrograde urethrogram first.
Persistent instability → pre-peritoneal packing / angio-embolisation / external fixation; then definitive orthopaedic fixation.
Then secondary survey (head-to-toe, AMPLE).
qs.why: An open-book pelvis can hide litres of blood in the pelvis; closing it with a binder over the trochanters reduces volume and tamponades venous bleeding. Pelvic fractures also tear the urethra, so no blind catheter until a retrograde urethrogram.

title: Aseptic technique, septic work-up & central line

qs.q: Describe the aseptic technique (e.g. for a central line).
a: Hand hygiene; cap, mask, sterile gown and gloves; skin antisepsis with chlorhexidine (let it dry); full-body sterile drape; sterile ultrasound probe cover; no-touch technique; sterile dressing.
qs.why: Central lines go straight into the bloodstream, so full sterile barrier precautions and chlorhexidine (allowed to dry) are what reduce catheter-related bloodstream infection.

qs.q: What is a septic work-up?
a: CBC with differential, CRP, lactate, blood cultures ×2 (before antibiotics), urine analysis & culture, CXR, cultures from any suspected source (wound, sputum, line tip),
U&E/LFT/coagulation.
qs.why: The septic work-up looks for the source and the severity: cultures must be taken before antibiotics, and lactate and organ tests show tissue hypoperfusion.

qs.q: Complications of a central line?
a: Immediate: arterial puncture, haematoma, pneumothorax/haemothorax, arrhythmia, air embolism, malposition.
Late: line infection / bacteraemia, thrombosis, catheter occlusion or fracture.
qs.why: Early complications come from the needle (artery, pleura, heart, air entry, wrong position); late ones from the catheter sitting in the vein (infection, thrombosis, blockage).
